Several methods can be used to estimate the mass of the
pump, which includes the method using the power density,
the empirical method, and the configuration design method.
The estimating method from the power density is simple,
but the mass estimation has low reliability when the selected
power density is invalid. The configuration design method
is the most accurate, but it is necessary to perform additional validations on whether the performance satisfies the
design conditions, such as mass flow rate, head rise, and efficiency. Moreover, it is inappropriate to perform this at the
conceptual design stage. Therefore, in this study, the mass
was estimated by an empirical method using existing pumps.
The 2D configuration of the one-stage centrifugal pump was
designed through the relationship between the flow characteristics and the impeller configuration. In addition, using
the diameter derived, the pump mass was estimated from the
diameter-mass trend line constructed from commercial centrifugal pumps. Figure 6 shows the design procedure and
results of the 2D configuration design. The configuration
design of the impeller was composed of a process of deriving
a 2D configuration from the mass flow rate, inlet pressure,
outlet pressure, rpm, efficiency, suction speed, blade thickness, and diameter ratio. The specific velocity and specific
diameter are defined using Eqs. (21–22), respectively, and the
outlet diameter was derived from Eq. (23) from the Cordier
diagram, which shows the empirical relationship between the
specific velocity and specific diameter. Because the relationship between the outlet diameter and the outlet velocity is
expressed by Eq. (24), the outlet velocity can be calculated,
and the outlet blade angle can be calculated from the velocity
triangle theory:

The motor, which is a component that rotates using electric energy, serves to transmit shaft power to the pump. The
power density, which is an important performance factor of

to the mass; hence, a high power density means high performance. Because the output power of the motor is the same
as the required pump power, the mass of the motor was calculated from Eqs. (26–27) using the pump power and motor
power density [1]:

**2.2** **Gas-Generator Cycle Modeling**

The gas-generator cycle is a method of driving a pump by
operating the turbine through the combustion gas generated
from the gas generator. Compared to the electric-pump cycle,
the gas- generator cycle does not require an electric motor
and inverter but requires additional components, such as gas
generators, flow control valves, and turbines. In this study,
the turbopump and gas-generator analysis modules were validated as reported elsewhere [16]. The components, except
for the gas generator and turbopump, were modeled similar
to that of the electric-pump cycle. Therefore, it was omitted
in this section. A mass estimation was newly performed in
this study. Figure 3b presents the analysis process of the gasgenerator cycle. The program initially assumed the mass flow
